extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and investigators of nature (readers of Baconian methodology)
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy of experimental 'instances' (ways of choosing or constructing observations/experiments) for investigating natural phenomena, explaining how to decide between causes, separate natures, and bring imperceptible things within the senses. Covers instances of the cross, divorce, lamp/door/citing instances, and practical instrumented reductions (microscope, telescope, weights, thermometer, distillation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the cross
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances used to decide between rival explanations by finding cases that favor one cause over another (cross-ways). These instances are meant to 'decide so far as to allow such a motion to be possible in nature' or, if absent in history/experiment, to 'suspect' a hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasting experiments or historical instances to discriminate between alternative accounts. Examples and suggested experiments given include: checking cometary motions to test diurnal motion hypotheses; clock experiments at different heights to test whether weight arises from attraction of the earth's mass; magnetic polarity experiments (placing a magnet under an untouched needle and observing whether earth or magnet dominates); optical experiments to test whether the moon is corporeal (reflection from rare bodies like flame); experiments on projectiles to decide whether motion is carried by air or by successive motion of body parts; analysis of gunpowder explosions to distinguish simple expansion from escaping 'crude spirit' and interacting bodies; experiments on flame to determine whether it is momentary because the cause ceases or because contrary natures destroy it (e.g., comparing nested flames of different colors to see whether an enclosed flame persists). The text emphasizes devising 'instances of the cross' for each debated nature and using careful observation/experimentation rather than speculative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of divorce
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that indicate the separation of a nature from a concrete substance with which it is usually found in conjunction; they show that one nature is capable of being separated from another without deciding which cause is primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use divorce instances to expose false forms and dissipate hasty theories. They 'decide nothing, but only inform us that the one nature is capable of being separated from the other.' Examples: heat, light, rarity, and motion appearing in different combinations (air is rare and movable but neither hot nor light; the moon is light but not hot; boiling water warm but not light). Magnetic attraction is cited as an instance of divorce of corporeal nature and natural action, with philosophical consequences about action at a distance and the possibility of incorporeal agency. Employ divorce instances to show that commonly associated properties can exist independently and thus challenge overly simple generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the lamp (immediate information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that 'assist the senses' and thus strengthen the direct path from sensory perception to understanding. They are divided into five classes: (1) strengthen, enlarge, and correct immediate operations of the senses; (2) reduce to the sphere of the senses matters beyond it; (3) indicate continued processes or series where only termini are usually observed; (4) supply the absolute wants of the senses; (5) excite attention and observation and limit subtilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instances are foundational because 'every interpretation of nature sets out from the senses.' The fivefold scheme directs experimenters to seek ways to improve sensory access, to render hidden processes observable, to recover series/processes instead of single outcomes, to supply missing sensory capabilities, and to direct attention appropriately. The passage presents this as a general organizing principle for experimental practice and emphasizes accumulation of accurate sensory representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the door or gate (helps to the senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of lamp-instances specifically aimed at assisting the immediate action of the senses: (1) enabling perception of objects not naturally seen; (2) seeing objects from a greater distance; (3) seeing more accurately and distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete instrument examples: microscopes (to perceive minute objects and latent minutiæ), telescopes (to see distant heavenly objects and details such as lunar features, Jupiter's satellites, sunspots), and measuring-rods/astrolabes (to correct and guide sight). The text notes limitations (microscopes only useful for minute objects; telescopic discoveries should be treated cautiously because few corroborating experiments exist). Use these 'doors' to expand and refine direct observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing/invoking instances (reducing objects to the sphere of the senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances used to 'cite' or 'invoke' things to appear which do not immediately fall within the senses — i.e., methods for reducing distant, concealed, minute, brief, violent, or otherwise imperceptible phenomena to observable signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize reasons objects escape the senses (distance, interposition, inaptness to impress, insufficient quantity, insufficient time, excessive violence, senses previously filled) and choose reduction tactics accordingly. Tactics include using substitutes detectable at a distance (fires, bells), reading surface signs (pulse, urine) to infer hidden states, making artful reductions (instrumentation, distillation, separations), and timing/measurement strategies. Examples: detecting 'spirit' in bodies via desiccation and weight loss, showing expansion of spirits (vapor) with the bladder-vial experiment, using a thermometer for slight heat/cold via air expansion, and artificial separations (distillation) to reveal composition (but with warnings that heat and violent agents can create artifacts and new qualities not originally present). The guidance strongly cautions against careless separations and stresses imitation/rivalry of nature rather than violent methods that induce fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to measurement and quantification (weights, tables, thermometers, instruments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instruments and quantification to make imperceptible or comparative properties manifest (e.g., weight-tables, bladder-vial vapor expansion experiment, thermometer, measuring-rods, astrolabes, microscopes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedures illustrated: compiling a table of weights and sizes for metals, minerals, liquids to reveal relations of density (noting a claimed ratio range among tangible bodies); measuring expansion of spirits of wine by vaporizing into a bladder to estimate volumetric change; employing the thermometer to detect weak degrees of heat or cold by air expansion/compression. The text treats such measurement as crucial for deriving 'density and rarity' and other hidden relations, but warns experimenters that some methods (especially heating/separation) may introduce qualities not originally present, so methods should imitate natural processes where possible and avoid violent agents that produce artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological injunction: judge nature by instances and enlightening experiments, not by 'probable reasons'
rubrics_metrics.description: A general methodological rule urging reliance on carefully constructed instances and experiments rather than speculative or merely probable reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed near the close of the cross-instances discussion: 'We have dwelt the longer upon them in order gradually to teach and accustom mankind to judge of nature by these instances, and enlightening experiments, and not by probable reasons.' This is a normative criterion for evaluating approaches to natural inquiry: favour controlled experiments and discriminating instances over purely speculative argumentation.
